title: The Mare on the Moor Road

poster.name: Sheila Bostock
idle: Looking for work, love? I've a small bother up at the farm, but it can wait until you've a badge in your pocket. Folk listen to a badge.
taken: Anything yet? My dog Moss won't cross the top field after teatime. He's a brave dog. He fetched a ewe out of a drain last spring.
decided: Sit down, pet. Kettle's on. Tell me what you made of it.
poster.closed: That's the top field sorted. Moss crossed it on Tuesday. I think he did it to be polite.
poster.haggle: Ha. You know your worth, and I know a good dog when I see one. Go on, then.

notice: Something big and white goes over the wall at the top field at dusk, no sound at all, then lets out a scream fit to curdle the milk.
Two walkers rang me in a state. The pub says it's the Wizard's mare, loose from the Edge. I say the Wizard can fetch his own horse.
trouble: It's in the Forest, on the lane up to the farm. Go at dusk, when it's about, and bring a torch you don't mind dropping.
I can't pay much. Moss and I just want the footpath back. The walkers have stopped coming and I miss the tea money.

clues.hint: the ground under a post by the lane
clues.text: No hoofprints anywhere, which is odd for a horse. But under the post lie little black pellets, glossy as liquorice, packed with tiny bones and a vole's skull. A mare does not bring up bones.

clues.hint: the top of the lane, watched at dusk or after dark
clues.text: You stand very still as the light goes. A pale shape drifts along the wall at head height, wings wide and utterly silent, and turns its flat white heart of a face towards you. Then it screams. It is smaller than a pony and a good deal ruder.
clues.hint_wait: Wall, sheep, a cold wind. Whatever comes here keeps late hours. Try again at dusk or after dark.

clues.hint: hear what the walker at the gate makes of it
text: The mare. Course it's the mare. White horse, no rider, comes over the wall like smoke. It's all in the story, a farmer and a white mare on the road to Macclesfield fair.
The old man in the cloak got that mare, and one of them has got out. You mark my words.
idle: I walk this lane every Sunday. I'm not scared. I just walk a bit faster at the top.
clues.after: An owl. Well, I never. Don't tell the pub. They'll be so disappointed.

clues.hint: ask the bird watcher with the binoculars
text: Pale from underneath, silent wings, a face like a heart, and a scream? Hares scream when they are caught, but they do not fly. That is a barn owl.
They do not hoot, you know. That is the tawny. The barn owl shrieks, and it has been frightening people in the dark for a very long time.
idle: Counting owls. There are fewer than there were. I'll tell you if I find one, but I'll not tell the pub.
clues.after: I'd rather folk were frightened of an owl than rid of one. I shall be putting that on a poster.

lair.name: The Mare
intro: The top of the lane, a drystone wall, and a gatepost as grey as the sky. A heap of black pellets sits underneath, and a smell of old hay.
Something pale and round-faced sits on the post and looks down at you without blinking. Sheila calls it the Mare. It has the air of a creature that has been called worse.
beaten: The Mare puffs up on the post, white face flat with outrage, and then goes silent and rather small. Down the lane, a dog barks once, bravely.

choices.label: Say nothing: let the Wizard's mare ride on
say: You tell Sheila it is only a ghost story and cannot be helped, and she says that is what she thought. By Sunday the pub has put a white horse on its sign, and the tea money is back.
The owl goes on hunting the top field, screaming at whoever walks into its evening. Nobody tells it that it is a horse.
poster: A mare, and not a word said? Grand. The pub's full, and I've sold forty scones to people looking for a ghost. Here's your fee.
after: Walkers ask me where the mare is. I point at the top field and say mind the wall. It's nearly true.
choices.journal: You let the legend stand. The footpath is full again and the pub has a white horse on its sign. The owl has never been told.

choices.label: Put up a barn owl box and a sign saying what it is
say: You and Sheila fix an owl box high in the hay barn and a small notice on the gate: BARN OWL. SILENT, SCREAMS, HARMLESS. Please do not look for the Wizard.
The walkers read the sign and stand very still at dusk. Half of them go home with the wrong end of a ghost story and the right end of an owl.
poster: An owl box and a sign. Folk stand at the gate with their phones out at dusk and say nothing. I can't believe how quiet it's got. Eighty per cent.
after: The owl uses the box. Moss has stopped minding the top field, and the tea money has come back for good. The pub is annoyed with me.
choices.journal: You fixed up a barn owl box and put a sign on the gate. The owl has a home, the walkers have a pastime, and the pub has lost its ghost.

choices.label: Leave it be: it is only an owl, and it will mind its own business
say: You tell Sheila what it is and walk away. She stands at the gate a long while, and then says she'll go up the top field after teatime herself, with Moss, and see.
Nothing eats anyone. The owl screams once, Moss growls once, and after a week they have come to an arrangement.
poster: An owl, and no fuss. Well, it's a relief. I'll go up with the dog and have a look myself. Sixty per cent, and a scone.
after: The owl and Moss have an understanding. He stays out of its way and it stays out of his. That's more than I can say for the pub.
choices.journal: You told Sheila it was an owl and left it at that. She faced it herself with her dog, and nobody was hurt.

choices.label: Catch it
say: The charm closes round the Mare, who goes in with a look of long-suffering dignity and a single, outraged hiss. A little way off, a dog barks once and then, very carefully, crosses the top field.
poster: It's in your team? A silent white owl that screams, in your team. Well, the top field's quiet. Eighty per cent. Don't let it near Moss.
after: Moss walks the top field like a lord now. I hear you've a barn owl with you. Does it still scream? I'd pay to see the Wizard's face.
choices.journal: You caught the Mare and now travel with a barn owl that screams. The top field is quiet, the pub is mournful, and Moss is insufferable.

real: Barn owls are pale underneath and fly almost silently, because the front edges of their feathers are soft and comb-like. They do not hoot: that is the tawny owl. A barn owl shrieks, and the white shape and the scream have probably started a good few haunting stories. Alderley Edge, near Macclesfield, has a legend of a farmer on his way to the fair with a white horse, who met an old man who led him into a cavern of sleeping knights, each with a white horse, with one short. Alan Garner built a children's book on it. Barn owls have lost many nesting sites as old barns are converted, and a box in a barn, set up high, is the usual help.

text: A fence post at the top of the lane, with a scatter of dark pellets at its foot.
The drystone wall at the top of the lane. The sheep have moved well away from it.

folk.name: Tea Room Owner
says: Sheila's scones, and a white horse on the pub sign. I've had three Americans ask for the Wizard. I told them he's at Alderley.
There's an owl box up at Sheila's now. They come for a look at dusk and stand about like a church. I sell a lot of tea.
Someone has a barn owl in their team that used to be the Mare. Sheila says it still screams. The pub doesn't know yet.
else: Sheila's scones. She says the top field's quiet now. She says it quietly, in case the owl is listening.
